items.passage: Fifteen years, two languages, one rule: an interpreter carries what is said, not what is meant. That rule brought me, Benedita, to the edge of a dirt soccer field on the plateau at dusk, beside Nova, a scout who had flown from Lisbon to meet the coach known across the region as a finder of talent. Nova had questions about drills and formations. The coach answered about roads. For twenty years, he said, he had driven the school van three hours each way on Saturdays to sheep camps without a road of their own, and he had never lost a player to distance. I put each sentence into Portuguese exactly; for once, what he said and what he meant were the same. Nova's pen stayed capped. When the light failed, the coach parked the van at the touchline and switched on its headlights, and the boys played on inside the two long beams, their shadows running ahead of them.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: A scout travels far to learn a celebrated coach's drills and formations for young players.
An interpreter's duty is to carry exactly what is said, setting aside what the speaker means.
Boys on a remote plateau love soccer so much that they will keep playing even after dark.
A coach's reputation for finding talent turns out to rest on years of patient, unseen effort.
items.recipeBeyondMedium: 요지가 세 곳의 근거를 종합해야 나오고, 오답은 각각 한 곳만 요약한 부분 요지다
items.explanation: 처음에 코치는 재능 발굴자로 알려져 있고 스카우트는 훈련법을 기대한다. 중간에서 코치는 전술 대신 20년간 도로 없는 목장까지 승합차를 몰았다는 이야기를 하고, 통역사는 이번만은 말과 뜻이 같았다고 뒤집어 말한다. 끝의 헤드라이트 장면도 같은 승합차가 경기를 이어 가게 하는 모습이어서, 명성이 보이지 않는 꾸준한 노력에 기대고 있다는 D가 정답이다. A는 처음 일화만, B는 중간의 통역 규칙만, C는 마지막 장면을 과장해 요지로 삼은 오답이다.

items.passage: Grapes have no business in Galway. Rory grows them anyway along the south wall of his workshop, and each October he presses them in a press he built before you, Aoife, became his apprentice. This year the press splits along one cheek. Rory has a glue for such repairs, made from a recipe he has never written down; for three years you have asked for it and been told you will learn it when you need it. He mixes it now while you watch, measuring nothing, talking about the weather. When you reach for a pencil, he sends you to the shed for clamps. Next morning he announces that his wrists are bad and the second batch is yours. You ruin it twice. On the third try he leans on the bench beside you, his wrists apparently healed, and tilts the pot a quarter-turn toward the window.
items.question: Based on the text, why does Rory most likely claim that his wrists are bad?
options: He is embarrassed that age has made his hands unsteady for delicate work.
He hopes the failed batches will keep the recipe safely his own.
He is worn out from a long season of harvesting and pressing grapes.
He wants Aoife to learn the recipe through her own hands, not notes.
items.recipeBeyondMedium: 동기를 한 문장에서 읽을 수 없고 떨어진 두 단서를 결합해야 하며, 오답이 한 단서만 설명하는 부분 정답이다
items.explanation: 앞부분에서 Rory는 비법은 필요할 때 배우게 된다고 말하고, Aoife가 연필을 집자 창고 심부름을 보내 기록을 막는다. 이후 그는 손목이 아프다며 두 번째 배치를 맡기는데, 세 번째 시도에서는 손목이 멀쩡한 채 옆에서 냄비를 빛 쪽으로 돌려 색을 보게 해 준다. 두 단서를 함께 설명하는 동기는 직접 만들어 보며 손으로 익히게 하려는 것이므로 D가 정답이다. A는 손목이 곧 나은 점과, B는 그가 결국 도와준다는 점과 충돌하며, C는 수확 시기라는 배경만 보고 고른 오답이다.

items.passage: What is owed to someone who leaves without a word and returns the same way? I turned that over at the bus depot in Gdansk, where my brother Marcus and I waited for our cousin Zofia, eleven years after she had boarded a night coach to Berlin. Marcus had polished his shoes and rehearsed, in the van, how the radio shop could use another pair of hands. I had rehearsed something sharper. She stepped down with one small bag, thinner than I remembered, kissed us both, and explained nothing. On the drive home she asked about every customer she could still name. I noticed that she flinched when the van door slammed and kept her bag on her knees the whole way. I did not say the sharp thing. At the depot behind us, a cleaner pushed a wide broom across bays stained with oil.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Zofia?
options: Softening, as the narrator senses what Zofia's absence may have cost her
Resentful, and still set on demanding an explanation for Zofia's long silence
Hopeful, mainly because Zofia might help rescue the failing radio shop
Wary, since the narrator suspects Zofia has come back only to ask for money
items.explanation: 화자는 처음에 날카로운 말을 준비해 왔다고 밝히지만, Zofia가 마른 모습으로 문소리에 움찔하고 가방을 무릎에서 놓지 않는 것을 눈여겨본다. 결국 화자는 준비한 날카로운 말을 하지 않는다. 이는 그녀가 겪었을 일을 짐작하며 마음이 누그러지는 태도이므로 A가 정답이다. B는 처음의 준비만 보고, C는 Marcus의 기대를 화자의 것으로, D는 근거 없는 의심으로 읽은 오답이다.

items.passage: Riccardo took the booth facing the door, as he always had back home, and ordered for both of them before Koa had opened the menu. Koa let him. On the drive from the motel Riccardo had mentioned, between songs on the radio, that at his new school the teachers still read his name off a list, and then he had laughed and turned the music up. When the plates came, the eggs Riccardo had ordered for Koa were pancakes; Koa saw it first, slid the plate toward himself, and said this was exactly what he had been craving. He asked for more coffee twice. Riccardo, telling a story about the school's vending machine, never noticed the waitress's apology. Outside, trucks threw spray across the lot, and the diner's sign buzzed and steadied.
items.question: Based on the text, which choice best describes the relationship between Koa and Riccardo?
options: Koa quietly protects Riccardo's pride while his friend struggles to adjust.
Riccardo looks after Koa, who is lonely and uncertain after the move.
Koa is losing patience with a friend who always orders for him without asking.
Riccardo and Koa compete, as old friends do, over who knows the other best.
items.recipeBeyondMedium: 두 문장의 단서를 연결해야 하고 오답은 한쪽 감정만 반영한다
items.explanation: 차 안에서 Riccardo는 새 학교에서 아직 아무도 자기 이름을 모른다고 말한 뒤 크게 웃으며 음악을 높인다. 식당에서 Koa는 주문 실수를 먼저 알아채고도 원하던 음식인 척하며 Riccardo가 실수를 모르고 지나가게 한다. 두 단서를 이으면 Koa가 친구의 자존심을 조용히 지켜 주는 관계이므로 A가 정답이다. B는 돌보는 방향을 거꾸로, C는 주문 습관만 보고 Koa의 불만으로, D는 일반적 통념으로 고른 오답이다.

items.passage: A clay jar, cracked through, rested on the floor of the salt-water pool in Colombo, where Alonso had dropped it showing off for the fishermen's boys. The old tellings say that a jar broken in the sea keeps the voice of the one who broke it. Alonso told his grandmother, Imtiaz, that a wave had knocked it from his arms. She did not argue. She waded in to her knees, lifted out a shard, and held it to his ear, then waited, looking at the water rather than at him. Alonso listened for a long time. At last he said the shard sounded like a boy who had been showing off. Imtiaz nodded once and pressed the shard into his palm to keep. Along the seawall, crows quarreled over a fish head in the noon glare.
items.question: Based on the text, which choice best describes the relationship between Imtiaz and Alonso?
options: Alonso fears Imtiaz, whose sternness leads him to invent excuses about the jar.
Imtiaz patiently leads Alonso toward honesty, and he answers her trust in kind.
Alonso teaches Imtiaz to hear the voices that the old tellings say jars keep.
Imtiaz indulges Alonso as grandmothers often do, excusing his every mistake.
items.recipeBeyondMedium: 두 문장의 단서를 연결해야 하고 오답은 한쪽 감정만 반영한다
items.explanation: Imtiaz는 Alonso의 핑계를 반박하지 않고, 조각을 그의 귀에 대 준 뒤 그를 보지 않고 기다려 준다. 그러자 Alonso는 스스로 자신이 뽐내다가 깼다고 인정하고, Imtiaz는 고개를 끄덕이며 조각을 그의 손에 쥐여 준다. 두 장면을 이으면 할머니가 인내심 있게 정직으로 이끌고 손자가 이에 응하는 관계이므로 B가 정답이다. A는 처음의 핑계만 보고, C는 방향을 거꾸로, D는 할머니에 대한 통념으로 고른 오답이다.

items.passage: Night makes people truthful. At the sanatorium above the lake outside Bergen, I was the nurse who sat up with the patients who could not sleep, and Thorvald was the most stubborn of them. He would not lie down until I wheeled him to the end of the dock, where he watched the water as if a boat were due. On the fourth night he told me about his brother, a quarrel over their father's boathouse, and a letter he had written the week after and carried in his coat ever since. His brother had died the following spring. I said that someone in the family might still read the letter, and he shook his head. An apology, he said, was a door that opens from one side only. After that he spoke less and slept more. When he asked me, Sigrid, to burn the envelope in the ward stove, I did, and I noticed that he no longer looked out at the water.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a door that opens from one side only” most nearly suggests that an apology is
options: a gesture Thorvald could make only after his brother first forgave him
a private confession that should stay hidden from everyone, even Sigrid
an act Thorvald had refused to begin because of his stubborn pride
an offering that needs someone living on the other side to receive it
items.explanation: Thorvald의 형은 이미 세상을 떠났고, 화자가 가족 중 누군가 편지를 읽을 수 있다고 하자 그는 고개를 젓는다. 이어서 그가 물 쪽을 바라보며 오지 않을 배를 기다리는 듯했다는 앞부분 묘사와 연결하면, 사과는 받아 줄 상대가 반대편에 있어야 완성된다는 뜻임을 알 수 있으므로 D가 정답이다. A는 용서의 순서를 거꾸로 해석한 오답이고, B는 편지를 태운 행동에만 기대어 비밀 유지로 오해한 것이다. C는 그가 편지를 이미 썼다는 사실과 맞지 않는다.

items.passage:
Who pays a clockmaker for the hours he gives away?
On Forty-Third Street my father, Santiago,
kept every clock in the window five minutes fast
so passersby would think themselves late and hurry in.
Ottavio came in January with his wife's watch,
mainspring snapped, the crystal fogged like breath on glass.
He laid his nickels out in a careful row.
My father slid them back across the counter
and bent above the bench past closing, past supper,
lending the stranger his own evening,
asking nothing on account.
I translated nothing. Nothing needed saying.
When the small heart started, Ottavio wept in Italian;
my father answered him in Spanish.
Neither man asked when the debt would come due.
I stood between them holding my English,
the one who believed words were the price of things.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “lending the stranger his own evening” most nearly suggests that Santiago was
options: giving up his own time without expecting anything in return
advancing his time to Ottavio on the promise of later payment
sacrificing family hours out of a shopkeeper's sense of duty
stretching the repair slowly to make the evening feel longer
items.explanation: Santiago는 Ottavio가 내민 동전을 돌려보내고 영업이 끝난 뒤에도 수리를 계속한다. 바로 뒤의 'asking nothing on account'와 뒷부분의 두 사람 모두 빚을 언제 갚을지 묻지 않았다는 구절을 함께 읽으면, '빌려준다'는 말은 대가 없이 자기 시간을 내주었다는 뜻이므로 A가 정답이다. B는 'lending'의 문자적 의미에 끌린 그럴듯한 오답이지만 지문이 대가를 기대하지 않았음을 두 번 보여 준다. C의 의무감과 D의 일부러 늦춘 수리는 지문에 근거가 없다.

items.passage:
Once the library on Central Avenue was ours,
its radiators ticking like patient clocks,
Elan at the window with the paper folded small
while I, Nayeli, wandered the stacks.
We had a system: I chose, he signed,
and neither of us called it trust.
One Saturday in March, between the atlases,
he mentioned that the house was sold,
Denver by June, the papers settled.
Settled, I said, admiring the word
the way one admires a stranger's handwriting.
Now I notice that the radiators hiss.
I notice how the books lean on one another
like people who have never been introduced.
I check out a road map, sign for it myself,
and practice the signature until it looks like someone older.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the poem?
options: From restless impatience to quiet acceptance of the planned move
From warm gratitude to open, tearful pleading with Elan to stay
From affectionate ease to guarded irony after the news
From shy uncertainty to growing excitement about a new life in Denver
items.explanation: 시의 앞부분은 '참을성 있는 시계' 같은 라디에이터와 Elan과의 익숙한 습관을 다정하게 그린다. 이사 소식 뒤에는 'Settled'라는 말을 낯선 사람의 글씨처럼 감상한다는 냉소적 표현, 라디에이터가 '쉭쉭거린다'는 변화, 혼자 서명하는 행동이 이어져 거리를 둔 아이러니한 어조로 바뀌므로 C가 정답이다. A는 화자가 겉으로 담담해 보이는 점에 끌린 오답이지만 그 담담함은 수용이 아니라 반어다. B의 눈물 어린 호소와 D의 설렘은 지문에 나타나지 않는다.

items.passage: By the seventh evening of the rains, the people of the lane had made a song about Kwesi. Up the stairs he went to Obinna's projection booth, always with the same cracked lens bundled in a cloth, and down he came with the lens glued and the song a verse longer. Obinna, who mended everything in the old Accra cinema, from ceiling fans to torn reels, played his part well. He sighed loudly, rolled his eyes for the children watching from the steps, and glued. Glass is like a promise, he told them; mend it once and it remembers the break. On the seventh evening, though, he raised the lens into the projector's beam to test his work, and the picture on the screen below came apart into two faces, one bright and one faint. Obinna lowered the lens. The children on the steps stopped singing without being told. In a voice the lane had never heard him use, he asked Kwesi whose film had last passed through this glass, and when Kwesi answered, Obinna wrapped the lens in his own handkerchief.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
options: From playful, communal teasing to a hushed and reverent stillness
From weary irritation with Kwesi to sudden anger at his deception
From gentle mockery of Obinna to admiring praise of his great skill
From cheerful curiosity about the lens to anxious fear of its strange power
items.explanation: 앞부분에서는 동네 사람들이 Kwesi에 대한 노래를 만들고 Obinna가 아이들 앞에서 과장되게 한숨 쉬며 눈을 굴리는 등 놀리는 분위기가 이어진다. 렌즈 속 화면이 두 얼굴로 갈라진 뒤에는 아이들이 저절로 노래를 멈추고, Obinna가 처음 듣는 목소리로 묻고, 렌즈를 자기 손수건에 싸는 행동이 나와 조용하고 경건한 분위기로 바뀌므로 A가 정답이다. B는 Obinna의 한숨을 진짜 짜증으로 읽은 오답이고, D는 화면이 갈라지는 장면을 공포로 오해한 것이다. C는 놀림의 대상이 Obinna가 아니라 Kwesi라는 점에서 틀렸다.

items.passage: We found the letters in a biscuit tin under the workbench of our mother's radio shop in Marrakesh, a week after the funeral. Yiannis read them aloud while I, Yasmin, sorted vacuum tubes into egg cartons. Each was from a man who signed with a single initial, thanking her for another repair she had refused to charge for, month after month, for eleven years. My brother set the last one down and looked at me, and I knew the word he was not saying. __She had always closed the shop an hour early on Thursdays, and she had never once told us where she went.__ For a while neither of us spoke. Then Yiannis turned the tin over, and a pamphlet slid out from beneath the paper lining: a schedule of Thursday evening readings at a school for the blind, with our mother listed as the volunteer who kept its radios working. The same initial was printed beside the director's name. Outside, the call to prayer rose over the rooftops, and Yiannis began, very carefully, to put the letters back in order.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It adds a detail that seems to deepen a suspicion later explained by a discovery.
It reveals that the narrator has long resented her mother's unexplained weekly absences.
It explains why the shop's earnings declined during the final years their mother ran it.
It offers decisive proof that their mother hid a romance from her children for years.
items.explanation: 밑줄 문장은 Yiannis가 말하지 않은 의심 바로 뒤에 놓여, 목요일마다 어머니가 사라졌다는 사실로 그 의심을 더 짙게 만든다. 그러나 뒤에서 발견된 팸플릿이 목요일 저녁 맹학교 낭독회와 어머니의 자원봉사, 같은 이니셜을 보여 주어 그 행적을 무해하게 설명하므로 A가 정답이다. D는 밑줄 문장만 따로 읽으면 그럴듯하지만 뒤의 발견과 맞지 않는다. B의 원망과 C의 가게 수입 감소는 지문에 근거가 없다.

items.passage: On the first Tuesday of each month, I fetched my younger brother Wolfram from a reading room near the Ringstrasse in Vienna, where his tutor, Anselm, taught him geography from maps older than our grandparents. Anselm was always late, he hummed while he corrected, and he would not let Wolfram use the tram diagram I had copied out for him. A boy should know a city by its faces, he said, its domes and fountains and shop signs, not by its numbered lines. I told my mother this was an old man's vanity. In February the trams stopped for two days in a snowstorm, and I went out in a panic and found Wolfram already halfway home, steering past the green church dome, the bakery's brass pretzel, the fountain with the chipped nose. I said nothing to Anselm about it the next Tuesday. He was late again, and humming. But I waited for him in the reading room instead of the cold hall, and on the walk home I let Wolfram choose the way.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Anselm?
options: Lasting suspicion, since she still doubts that his methods kept Wolfram safe
Open gratitude, since she thanks him warmly for preparing Wolfram so well
Grudging respect, shown more in her actions than in anything she tells him
Weary tolerance, since his lateness and humming still outweigh his lessons
items.explanation: 화자는 처음에 Anselm의 지도법을 노인의 허영이라 여겼지만, 눈보라 속에서 Wolfram이 그가 가르친 랜드마크로 길을 찾는 것을 본다. 그 뒤 그녀는 Anselm에게 아무 말도 하지 않으면서도 추운 복도 대신 열람실에서 기다리고 동생에게 길을 고르게 하는 행동으로 인정을 드러내므로 C가 정답이다. D는 Anselm이 여전히 늦고 흥얼거린다는 서술에 끌린 그럴듯한 오답이지만, 화자의 행동 변화를 설명하지 못한다. B는 그녀가 아무 말도 하지 않았다는 점과, A는 눈보라 장면의 결과와 맞지 않는다.

items.passage: Who should stay behind when the olives go down to market? So begin the tellers on the terraces above Naples, and so began young Emilio, newly sent to the hill school, who answered the question with great confidence. The slowest reader, he declared, would stay to mind the trees. Alessia read slowly and counted faster than the priest. She folded her arms and stayed. By noon the baskets at market were tallied wrong, the prices tangled, and Emilio was climbing back up the hill with his collar undone, a climb the tellers describe at length and with evident pleasure. They are careful to add that he asked Alessia's pardon before he asked her help, and that the following year he chose by drawing lots. Some insist he never admitted the error aloud; others say he admitted it only to the trees. Grandmothers telling it still pause here to slice the bread.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Emilio?
options: Stern disapproval, presenting his decision as a lasting stain on the school
Quiet admiration, presenting his first choice as sensible in the circumstances
Fond amusement, relishing his embarrassment while crediting his reform
Cool neutrality, recounting his actions without favoring any version of events
items.explanation: 화자는 Emilio가 옷깃을 풀어헤친 채 언덕을 다시 오르는 장면을 이야기꾼들이 길게, 즐겁게 묘사한다고 전하며 그의 망신을 즐긴다. 동시에 그가 도움을 청하기 전에 먼저 Alessia에게 용서를 구했고 이듬해에는 제비뽑기로 정했다는 점을 '조심스럽게 덧붙여' 그의 변화를 인정하므로 C가 정답이다. D는 서로 다른 판본을 나란히 소개하는 부분에 끌린 그럴듯한 오답이지만, 화자의 어조는 중립적이지 않다. A의 엄한 비난과 B의 첫 선택에 대한 칭찬은 지문과 맞지 않는다.

items.passage: On the Thursday after the funeral, Josiah carried his late teacher's violin into the laundromat because he had nowhere else to wait while his shirts dried. Harriet, who conducted the youth orchestra, was folding towels two machines away. Everyone had assumed the old man would leave the instrument to her, his oldest student, not to a fourteen-year-old who still rushed his scales. Josiah offered to give it to her. Harriet looked at the dented case, then asked him to play something. She listened through two cycles of the dryers without correcting a note, and afterward she wrote down the name of a shop that restrings old violins cheaply. Outside, a bus hissed at the curb, and steam from the vents curled into the cold air.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: A teenage violinist practices in a laundromat while he waits for his laundry.
A conductor tests a young player to decide whether he may join her orchestra.
Grief is best eased when people share the music that the departed loved.
A musician passed over in a bequest comes to support its young recipient.
items.recipeBeyondMedium: 두 곳의 근거를 합쳐 요지를 잡아야 하고, 오답 하나는 일화 요약에 그치는 부분 요지다
items.explanation: 앞부분에서 모두가 바이올린이 가장 오래된 제자인 Harriet에게 갈 것이라 예상했다는 사실이 제시된다. 뒷부분에서 Harriet은 Josiah가 바이올린을 넘기겠다고 해도 받지 않고, 연주를 고쳐 주지 않고 들은 뒤 현을 싸게 가는 가게를 알려 주어 그를 돕는다는 대비가 나오므로 D가 정답이다. A는 일화의 겉모습만 요약했고, B는 Harriet의 시험이라는 다른 목적을 끌어왔다. C는 지문 소재를 지나치게 일반화한 교훈이다.

items.passage: "Still just looking at it?" Devon called from the end of the dock. Amelie did not turn around. The half-built skiff had sat on its sawhorses beside the lake for nine summers, since the evening the two of them had argued over the bow and each walked off certain of being right. Last week she had taken out her old sketches and found, in the margin of the bow drawing, a note in Devon's handwriting she had never read: try it your way first. This evening she brought her plane and a jar of nails, ran her palm along the curve he had wanted, and set the plane down untouched. When he came near, she held out a second hammer, handle first. A heron lifted from the reeds and flew low toward the cypresses.
items.question: Based on the text, why does Amelie most likely hold out a second hammer to Devon?

She is still hurt by his teasing and wants him to do the hardest work alone.

items.passage: When I was twelve, I snapped my father's bicycle chain on a Dhaka curb and carried the pieces to Hari's shoe repair stall, rehearsing a story about a careless rickshaw driver. Hari, my father's oldest friend, did not ask what had happened. He told me to hold one end of the chain steady, Putri, steady, and while he worked the links he described a sandal he had torn as a boy and the stray dog he had blamed for it. His father, he said, still warns the grandchildren about that dog. Hari laughed when he said it, but he kept his eyes on the wire. That evening I told my father I had jumped the curb too fast. She hopes her father will laugh about it the way Hari laughed about the dog.

items.passage: Oaxaca was dry that March, and the river below my grandmother's village had shrunk to stones and cracked mud. Halfway across, Esperanza stopped and asked me to say my whole name. I said Eulalio, the name on my school papers. She waited, so I added the second one, which my parents had written on my birth record and never used. She asked me to say it again, louder, and then again. Years later I learned it had been her younger brother's, lost at this crossing in a high-water season, and that she was the last in the village who still spoke it. items.question: Based on the text, why does Esperanza most likely make Eulalio repeat his second name?

"Translate only what I say," Somchai told me the first morning, and so I have, Mother, for six weeks in this printing room in Chiang Mai. Yesterday the investors asked who had designed the new press. Somchai glanced at the young mechanic oiling the rollers and said the design was his own. I had seen the mechanic's drawings pinned above his bench, and for a moment I nearly said so. Then I remembered that on my first day the same investors had asked which workers came from families who owed them money, and that the mechanic had gone pale and left the room. I translated Somchai's claim word for word. My face burned the whole afternoon. This morning the presses started early, and the room smells of ink and wet paper. items.passage: I, Faris, found the letters on our third day snowed into the cabin above Beirut, tucked under the lining of my grandfather's desk drawer. Every one was addressed to Noor, his oldest friend, who was waiting out the storm with us, and none had been sent. In them he admitted that a prize-winning poem from their student years had been hers, not his. Noor sat knitting by the stove. Twice that week I had heard her remark that my grandfather never once apologized for anything, and both times she laughed as if it did not matter. ### lit40-hard-01-096 — skill central_ideas_details · 유형 main_idea_or_purpose
[지문]
Fifteen years, two languages, one rule: an interpreter carries what is said, not what is meant. That rule brought me, Benedita, to the edge of a dirt soccer field on the plateau at dusk, beside Nova, a scout who had flown from Lisbon to meet the coach known across the region as a finder of talent. Nova had questions about drills and formations. The coach answered about roads. For twenty years, he said, he had driven the school van three hours each way on Saturdays to sheep camps without a road of their own, and he had never lost a player to distance. I put each sentence into Portuguese exactly; for once, what he said and what he meant were the same. Nova's pen stayed capped. When the light failed, the coach parked the van at the touchline and switched on its headlights, and the boys played on inside the two long beams, their shadows running ahead of them.

[질문] Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
A) A scout travels far to learn a celebrated coach's drills and formations for young players.
B) An interpreter's duty is to carry exactly what is said, setting aside what the speaker means.
C) Boys on a remote plateau love soccer so much that they will keep playing even after dark.
D) A coach's reputation for finding talent turns out to rest on years of patient, unseen effort.

[표시된 정답] D
[해설]
처음에 코치는 재능 발굴자로 알려져 있고 스카우트는 훈련법을 기대한다. 중간에서 코치는 전술 대신 20년간 도로 없는 목장까지 승합차를 몰았다는 이야기를 하고, 통역사는 이번만은 말과 뜻이 같았다고 뒤집어 말한다. 끝의 헤드라이트 장면도 같은 승합차가 경기를 이어 가게 하는 모습이어서, 명성이 보이지 않는 꾸준한 노력에 기대고 있다는 D가 정답이다. A는 처음 일화만, B는 중간의 통역 규칙만, C는 마지막 장면을 과장해 요지로 삼은 오답이다.
### lit40-hard-01-100 — skill inferences · 유형 character_motivation
[지문]
Grapes have no business in Galway. Rory grows them anyway along the south wall of his workshop, and each October he presses them in a press he built before you, Aoife, became his apprentice. This year the press splits along one cheek. Rory has a glue for such repairs, made from a recipe he has never written down; for three years you have asked for it and been told you will learn it when you need it. He mixes it now while you watch, measuring nothing, talking about the weather. When you reach for a pencil, he sends you to the shed for clamps. Next morning he announces that his wrists are bad and the second batch is yours. You ruin it twice. On the third try he leans on the bench beside you, his wrists apparently healed, and tilts the pot a quarter-turn toward the window.

[질문] Based on the text, why does Rory most likely claim that his wrists are bad?
A) He is embarrassed that age has made his hands unsteady for delicate work.
B) He hopes the failed batches will keep the recipe safely his own.
C) He is worn out from a long season of harvesting and pressing grapes.
D) He wants Aoife to learn the recipe through her own hands, not notes.

[표시된 정답] D
[해설]
앞부분에서 Rory는 비법은 필요할 때 배우게 된다고 말하고, Aoife가 연필을 집자 창고 심부름을 보내 기록을 막는다. 이후 그는 손목이 아프다며 두 번째 배치를 맡기는데, 세 번째 시도에서는 손목이 멀쩡한 채 옆에서 냄비를 빛 쪽으로 돌려 색을 보게 해 준다. 두 단서를 함께 설명하는 동기는 직접 만들어 보며 손으로 익히게 하려는 것이므로 D가 정답이다. A는 손목이 곧 나은 점과, B는 그가 결국 도와준다는 점과 충돌하며, C는 수확 시기라는 배경만 보고 고른 오답이다.
### lit40-medium-01-005 — skill central_ideas_details · 유형 narrator_attitude
[지문]
What is owed to someone who leaves without a word and returns the same way? I turned that over at the bus depot in Gdansk, where my brother Marcus and I waited for our cousin Zofia, eleven years after she had boarded a night coach to Berlin. Marcus had polished his shoes and rehearsed, in the van, how the radio shop could use another pair of hands. I had rehearsed something sharper. She stepped down with one small bag, thinner than I remembered, kissed us both, and explained nothing. On the drive home she asked about every customer she could still name. I noticed that she flinched when the van door slammed and kept her bag on her knees the whole way. I did not say the sharp thing. At the depot behind us, a cleaner pushed a wide broom across bays stained with oil.

[질문] Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Zofia?
A) Softening, as the narrator senses what Zofia's absence may have cost her
B) Resentful, and still set on demanding an explanation for Zofia's long silence
C) Hopeful, mainly because Zofia might help rescue the failing radio shop
D) Wary, since the narrator suspects Zofia has come back only to ask for money

[표시된 정답] A
[해설]
화자는 처음에 날카로운 말을 준비해 왔다고 밝히지만, Zofia가 마른 모습으로 문소리에 움찔하고 가방을 무릎에서 놓지 않는 것을 눈여겨본다. 결국 화자는 준비한 날카로운 말을 하지 않는다. 이는 그녀가 겪었을 일을 짐작하며 마음이 누그러지는 태도이므로 A가 정답이다. B는 처음의 준비만 보고, C는 Marcus의 기대를 화자의 것으로, D는 근거 없는 의심으로 읽은 오답이다.
### lit40-medium-01-032 — skill inferences · 유형 relationship_between_characters
[지문]
Riccardo took the booth facing the door, as he always had back home, and ordered for both of them before Koa had opened the menu. Koa let him. On the drive from the motel Riccardo had mentioned, between songs on the radio, that at his new school the teachers still read his name off a list, and then he had laughed and turned the music up. When the plates came, the eggs Riccardo had ordered for Koa were pancakes; Koa saw it first, slid the plate toward himself, and said this was exactly what he had been craving. He asked for more coffee twice. Riccardo, telling a story about the school's vending machine, never noticed the waitress's apology. Outside, trucks threw spray across the lot, and the diner's sign buzzed and steadied.

[질문] Based on the text, which choice best describes the relationship between Koa and Riccardo?
A) Koa quietly protects Riccardo's pride while his friend struggles to adjust.
B) Riccardo looks after Koa, who is lonely and uncertain after the move.
C) Koa is losing patience with a friend who always orders for him without asking.
D) Riccardo and Koa compete, as old friends do, over who knows the other best.

[표시된 정답] A
[해설]
차 안에서 Riccardo는 새 학교에서 아직 아무도 자기 이름을 모른다고 말한 뒤 크게 웃으며 음악을 높인다. 식당에서 Koa는 주문 실수를 먼저 알아채고도 원하던 음식인 척하며 Riccardo가 실수를 모르고 지나가게 한다. 두 단서를 이으면 Koa가 친구의 자존심을 조용히 지켜 주는 관계이므로 A가 정답이다. B는 돌보는 방향을 거꾸로, C는 주문 습관만 보고 Koa의 불만으로, D는 일반적 통념으로 고른 오답이다.
### lit40-medium-01-037 — skill inferences · 유형 relationship_between_characters

A clay jar, cracked through, rested on the floor of the salt-water pool in Colombo, where Alonso had dropped it showing off for the fishermen's boys. The old tellings say that a jar broken in the sea keeps the voice of the one who broke it. Alonso told his grandmother, Imtiaz, that a wave had knocked it from his arms. She did not argue. She waded in to her knees, lifted out a shard, and held it to his ear, then waited, looking at the water rather than at him. Alonso listened for a long time. At last he said the shard sounded like a boy who had been showing off. Imtiaz nodded once and pressed the shard into his palm to keep. Along the seawall, crows quarreled over a fish head in the noon glare.

asking nothing on account.
